key_terms.meaning: At equilibrium p<sub>A</sub> = H x<sub>A</sub>, or for dilute systems y<sub>A</sub> = m x<sub>A</sub>, linking gas partial pressure to liquid concentration.
Pressure per unit liquid mole fraction; m = H/P is the dimensionless equilibrium slope.
Plot of solute-free gas ratio Y = mol solute/mol carrier gas against liquid ratio X = mol solute/mol solvent.
Locus of Y* in equilibrium with X; for dilute absorption Y* = mX.
Solute balance between any point and one end of the absorber; for dilute counter-current absorption Y = (L/G)X + constant.
Vertical gap Y − Y* at a given X, or X* − X at a given Y.
Smallest L/G that can reach the specified Y<sub>out</sub>; the operating line touches the equilibrium line.
Point where operating and equilibrium lines touch at minimum solvent; driving force is zero.
Gas and liquid flow in the same direction; operating line moves toward equilibrium and driving force falls along the column.
Gas and liquid flow in opposite directions; operating line stays farther from equilibrium, giving larger average driving force.
Gas contacts fresh liquid in successive stages; several operating lines or a stepped path, not one straight line.
A = L/(mG), ratio of operating-line slope to equilibrium-line slope; A > 1 gives finite stage count.
Analytical relation between N, A and solute recovery for straight equilibrium and operating lines.
Total packing surface per unit volume of packed bed, m²/m³; the wetted area is at most this.
Fraction of packed-bed volume that is empty, dimensionless.
Empirical packing characteristic used in pressure-drop and capacity correlations.
Height of an overall gas-phase transfer unit, m; includes gas and liquid film resistances.
Number of overall gas-phase transfer units, dimensionless; set by equilibrium and operating lines.
Absorption in which heat of solution changes liquid temperature and hence solubility.
E = actual absorption rate with reaction ÷ physical absorption rate without reaction.
Transfer of one or more gas components into a liquid solvent.
Removal of dissolved gas from a liquid by contact with a gas lean in that solute.
Moles of solute per mole of carrier gas or solvent, excluding the solute itself.
An ideal contact stage in which outgoing gas and liquid are in equilibrium.
Ratio of actual solute removed on a tray to solute removed by an ideal theoretical stage.
Packed height per theoretical stage, m; for straight lines HETP = H<sub>OG</sub> ln λ/(λ − 1), λ = mG/L.

K<sub>Ya</sub>: overall gas-phase coefficient times interfacial area per bed volume, kmol/(m³·s·ΔY); H<sub>OG</sub> = G<sub>M</sub>/(K<sub>Ya</sub>) and 1/(K<sub>Ya</sub>) = 1/(k<sub>Ya</sub>) + m/(k<sub>Xa</sub>).
Absorption in which the dissolved solute reacts chemically with the solvent or a reagent in it.
Ha = √(kD<sub>A</sub>)/k<sub>L</sub>: reaction in the film against diffusion through it; Ha > 3 fast (E ≈ Ha), Ha < 0.3 slow (E ≈ 1).
Trays change composition in steps (count stages); packed, spray and bubble columns change it continuously (integrate over height).

takeaways: Solubility fixes equilibrium, and Henry's law turns dilute gas-liquid equilibrium into a straight line on a Y–X plot.
The operating line is a solute balance; the vertical gap between it and the equilibrium line is the driving force.
The minimum liquid-to-gas ratio occurs when the operating line touches the equilibrium line at a pinch.
Counter-current contact gives more average driving force than co-current contact and is the usual choice for absorption.
The absorption factor A = L/(mG) measures how far the liquid rate exceeds the minimum and controls the number of stages.
Packing area a, void fraction ε and packing factor Fp decide interfacial area, capacity and pressure drop.
Packed height Z = H<sub>OG</sub> × N<sub>OG</sub> separates the mass-transfer coefficient from the separation duty.
Heat release raises liquid temperature and lowers solubility; reaction consumes solute and raises the rate through E.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine the equilibrium and operating lines, the minimum solvent rate, a stage or NTU–HTU design and a comment on thermal or reactive effects; multicomponent absorption and absorption with reaction are asked as separate questions in most syllabi.

bank.q: State Henry's law in the form p<sub>A</sub> = H x<sub>A</sub> and explain how it becomes Y* = mX on a solute-free plot.
outline: define p<sub>A</sub>, x<sub>A</sub> and H
convert dilute y = m x to Y ≈ y and X ≈ x
straight equilibrium line through the origin for dilute absorption
effect of temperature on H and m
answer: Henry's law. For a dilute solution of a gas that does not react with the solvent, the partial pressure of solute A over the liquid is proportional to its mole fraction in the liquid: p<sub>A</sub> = H x<sub>A</sub>. p<sub>A</sub> is in atm (or bar), x<sub>A</sub> is the liquid mole fraction and H is Henry's constant in atm per mole fraction. H depends on the solute, the solvent and the temperature, not on the total pressure. A concentration form p<sub>A</sub> = H'c<sub>A</sub> also exists, with H' in atm·m³/kmol; quote the form with the number.

From pressure to mole fractions. In the gas, p<sub>A</sub> = y<sub>A</sub> P (Dalton), where P is the total pressure. Equating, y<sub>A</sub> P = H x<sub>A</sub> at equilibrium, so y* = (H/P) x = m x. The slope m = H/P is dimensionless. Example from the solubility chapter: SO₂ in water with H = 40 atm per mole fraction gives m = 40 at 1 atm and m = 20 at 2 atm, so raising the pressure lowers m and helps absorption.

From mole fractions to mole ratios. In an absorber the carrier gas G (kmol/h) and the solute-free solvent L (kmol/h) do not change from top to bottom, so design uses Y = y/(1 − y) and X = x/(1 − x). Substituting y = Y/(1 + Y) and x = X/(1 + X) into y = mx gives Y/(1 + Y) = mX/(1 + X), which is a curve. For dilute systems (y and x below about 0.05) 1 + Y ≈ 1 and 1 + X ≈ 1, so Y* ≈ mX, a straight line through the origin of the Y–X plot.

answer.text: Check of the dilute approximation for m = 2 (the acetone example of this unit):

answer: Temperature. H rises with temperature for nearly all gases, so m rises and the equilibrium line steepens: warm solvent holds less gas at the same gas composition. For acetone in water m rises about 4 % per kelvin, so a liquid that warms 7 K moves m from 2.0 to about 2.56. Absorbers are therefore fed with cool solvent and strippers are heated.

Limits. Henry's law fails for concentrated solutions and describes only the physically dissolved part of a gas that reacts (SO₂, NH₃, CO₂ in water); then measured equilibrium data are plotted as a curve.

Closing check. For y = 0.08 at 1 atm, x = 0.08 × 1/40 = 0.002; at 2 atm, x = 0.16/40 = 0.004, twice as much. On Y–X axes with m = 2, X = 0.0175 gives Y* = 0.035 by the straight line against 0.0356 exactly, within 2 %, so the straight line is fair for this unit's examples.

bank.q: Compare co-current, counter-current and cross-current gas-liquid contact for absorption. Include operating-line shape and average driving force.
outline: co-current: same direction, operating line ends at equilibrium, low driving force
counter-current: opposite directions, largest average driving force, standard absorber
cross-current: gas contacts fresh liquid in stages, no single straight operating line
choice depends on recovery, solvent rate and pressure drop
answer: Co-current. Gas and liquid enter at the same end and leave together at the other. A balance from the inlet gives G(Y<sub>in</sub> − Y) = L(X − X<sub>in</sub>), a straight line of slope −L/G on Y–X axes. Its best possible end is equilibrium at the outlet, Y<sub>out</sub> = mX<sub>out</sub>, so X<sub>out</sub> = Y<sub>in</sub>/(m + L/G) for fresh solvent. Adding stages only brings the outlet closer to that point; it can never pass it.

Counter-current. Rich gas enters at the bottom and lean solvent at the top. The operating line Y = Y<sub>out</sub> + (L/G)(X − X<sub>in</sub>) has slope +L/G and runs from (X<sub>in</sub>, Y<sub>out</sub>) at the top to (X<sub>out</sub>, Y<sub>in</sub>) at the bottom. Fresh liquid meets the leanest gas and the richest liquid meets the richest gas, so a driving force exists at both ends as long as L/G is above the minimum.

Cross-current. The gas passes from stage to stage and every stage gets its own fresh solvent, which leaves from that stage. Each stage has a short operating line starting from X<sub>0</sub>, so the path is a set of segments, not one line. The first contact in each stage has a large driving force, but the solvent leaves each stage weak, so the total solvent is much larger. It is used in extraction and leaching, rarely in absorption.

answer.text: Worked comparison with the chapter's numbers: Y<sub>in</sub> = 0.0526, X<sub>in</sub> = 0, Y* = 2X, L/G = 2.105.

answer: Average driving force. Counter-current keeps the gap Y − Y* open from end to end (0.00503 at the top, 0.0074 at the bottom here), so its average is the largest and it needs the fewest stages for a given duty. Co-current's gap closes to zero at the outlet, so its average is small. Cross-current starts each stage with a large gap but ends each with a small one.

Choice. Counter-current for normal absorption and stripping (packed and tray towers). Co-current when a fast irreversible reaction removes the solute so equilibrium does not limit the outlet, or when a short, high-velocity contact is wanted, as in a venturi scrubber; it also avoids flooding because both streams move the same way. Cross-current where fresh solvent is cheap or each stage must start clean.
Closing check. With the same solvent, co-current leaves Y<sub>out</sub> = 0.0256 against counter-current's 0.00503, a ratio 0.0256/0.00503 = 5.1: counter-current gives a gas five times leaner.

bank.q: Define absorption factor A = L/(mG). Explain how its value controls the number of theoretical stages.
outline: L and G are solute-free liquid and gas rates
m is the equilibrium-line slope
A > 1 gives finite stages; A near 1 needs many stages
Kremser equation links A, N and recovery
answer: Definition. A = L/(mG), where L is the solute-free solvent flow (kmol/h), G the inert gas flow (kmol/h) and m the slope of the equilibrium line Y* = mX. A is the slope of the operating line, L/G, divided by the slope of the equilibrium line, m. It is dimensionless. Its inverse is the stripping factor S = mG/L.

Meaning on the Y–X plot. A > 1: the operating line is steeper than the equilibrium line, the two lines diverge towards the rich end, and the gap grows down the column. A = 1: the lines are parallel and every step is the same size. A < 1: the lines converge towards the rich end; with fresh solvent the column can absorb at most a fraction A of the solute even with infinite stages.

Physical picture. Each theoretical stage takes the gas from Y<sub>n</sub>+1 down to Y<sub>n</sub> and the liquid from X<sub>n</sub>−1 up to X<sub>n</sub>. How far one stage moves the compositions depends on the gap between the two lines. A large A keeps the operating line far above the equilibrium line at the rich end, so the bottom stages make big steps; a small A crowds the lines together and every step shrinks.

Graphical view. On the Y–X plot the stages are the horizontal-and-vertical steps between the operating line Y = Y<sub>1</sub> + (L/G)(X − X<sub>0</sub>) and Y* = mX, starting at the top (X<sub>0</sub>, Y<sub>1</sub>). Counting steps until Y reaches Y<sub>N</sub>+1 gives N, which is what the Kremser equation does in closed form when both lines are straight.

Kremser equation. For straight lines and X<sub>0</sub> = 0, the fraction absorbed in N theoretical stages is R = (A<sup>N+1</sup> − A)/(A<sup>N+1</sup> − 1). Solved for N: N + 1 = ln[(A − R)/(1 − R)]/ln A, and at A = 1, N = R/(1 − R).

answer.text: Stages for R = 0.90 at several A (Kremser, natural logs):

answer: How A controls N. Just above A = 1 a little extra solvent cuts the stage count sharply (1.05 → 1.20 saves 2.3 stages). Beyond about A = 1.5 the curve is flat (1.5 → 2.0 saves one stage) while the solvent rate rises by a third. That is why absorbers are designed at A = 1.25 to 1.5, and why A = R (here 0.9) is the absolute minimum: there the stage count is infinite.

Worked case. L/G = 2.72 and m = 2 give A = 1.36. For 90 % removal, (1.36 − 0.90)/0.10 = 4.60, N + 1 = ln 4.60/ln 1.36 = 1.5261/0.3075 = 4.963, N = 3.96. Stepping off on the Y–X plot gives Y = 0.00526, 0.01241, 0.02214, 0.03537 and then 0.0534 > 0.0526 after the fourth step, which agrees.

Closing check. With E<sub>o</sub> = 0.60 the column needs 3.96/0.60 = 6.6, so 7 real trays. Assumptions: straight equilibrium line, constant L/G, isothermal operation; a hot or concentrated system needs a stage-by-stage calculation.

bank.q: Define specific surface a, void fraction ε and packing factor Fp for a tower packing. State one design use of each.
outline: a is the total packing surface per packed volume (the wetted area is at most this)
ε is the empty volume fraction
F<sub>p</sub> is an empirical pressure-drop characteristic
a gives interfacial area; ε gives capacity; F<sub>p</sub> gives pressure drop and flooding
answer: Specific surface a: the total surface of the packing pieces per unit volume of packed bed, m²/m³ (a = A<sub>p</sub>/V<sub>bed</sub>). The wetted area that actually transfers mass is at most this and falls when liquid channels. Design use: interfacial area for mass transfer, a sits inside K<sub>Ya</sub>, so a larger a gives a smaller H<sub>OG</sub> and a shorter bed.

Void fraction ε: the empty volume of the bed divided by the bed volume, dimensionless (ε = V<sub>void</sub>/V<sub>bed</sub>). Random rings and saddles have about 0.70 to 0.95, metal structured sheet 0.95 to 0.98. Design use: capacity. More void leaves more room for gas and liquid, so the flooding gas rate is higher and the pressure drop lower.

Packing factor F<sub>p</sub>: an empirical number for each packing type and size, in m⁻¹ (older charts in ft⁻¹), fitted from measured pressure drops; it grows roughly as a/ε³ and rises as pieces get smaller. Design use: pressure drop and flooding. It is read into the generalised pressure-drop correlation to find the flooding gas rate and the pressure drop at the design rate.

Why all three are needed. A packing with a large a but a small ε gives plenty of area but floods at a low gas rate, so the column must be wide; one with a large ε but a small a has capacity but transfers little per metre, so the column must be tall. F<sub>p</sub> ties both into the pressure-drop chart, which fixes the diameter, while a (through K<sub>Ya</sub> and H<sub>OG</sub>) fixes the height.
Materials. Ceramic for corrosive and hot service, plastic for cheap low-temperature duty, metal where high capacity and thin walls (high ε) matter.

Trade-off. Smaller pieces give more a (better transfer) but also a larger F<sub>p</sub> (more pressure drop, lower flooding rate). Larger pieces give the opposite. Rule: piece size below about one-eighth of the column diameter, so the bed packs evenly at the wall.

Worked use (packed-tower example): a 1.2 m column with 4 m of 25 mm rings, a = 200 m²/m³, ε = 0.75. A<sub>c</sub> = π(1.2)²/4 = 1.131 m²; V<sub>bed</sub> = 4.524 m³; surface = 200 × 4.524 = 904.8 m²; voids = 0.75 × 4.524 = 3.393 m³.

Closing check. Switching to 50 mm rings (a = 100 m²/m³) leaves 100 × 4.524 = 452.4 m², half the surface: the bed would need to be about twice as tall for the same duty if K<sub>Ya</sub> scales with a, but the pressure drop per metre would be much lower.

bank.q: Explain why non-isothermal absorption can reduce or destroy the driving force in a packed absorber.
outline: heat of solution raises liquid temperature
solubility falls as temperature rises
equilibrium line moves up or becomes curved
driving force shrinks; a temperature bulge may appear
answer: Heat release. Solute entering the liquid gives up its heat of solution (and its latent heat if it is a condensable vapour). With little heat loss the liquid warms as it flows down: ΔT = (solute absorbed × ΔH<sub>s</sub>)/(liquid mass flow × c<sub>p</sub>).
Solubility falls with temperature. H, and so m = H/P, rises with temperature. At any liquid composition the equilibrium gas composition Y* = mX is higher in warm liquid.

Where the effect is largest. The liquid is coolest at the top (fresh solvent) and hottest at the bottom, where it has absorbed the most solute. So the equilibrium line stays near its cold position at the lean end and curves upward towards the rich end. The operating line, a balance on solute-free flows, does not move.

answer.text: Numbers from the acetone example: 4.52 kmol/h absorbed into 258 kmol/h water, ΔH<sub>s</sub> = 30 000 kJ/kmol, c<sub>p</sub> = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K), m rising 4 % per K.

answer: Consequence for design. The bottom driving force is less than half the isothermal value, so N<sub>OG</sub> rises; integrating ∫dY/(Y − Y*) with the warm equilibrium line gives 6.06 instead of 4.75, a bed of 1.82 m instead of 1.42 m. If the heat effect were larger, or the solvent rate close to the minimum, the curved equilibrium line could touch the operating line: the driving force is destroyed and no height reaches the specification.

Temperature bulge. When the entering gas is cold and the solvent evaporates, the gas can cool the liquid at the bottom and carry heat upward, so the hottest point lies inside the column; the pinch can then form part way up.
Remedies: more solvent (smaller ΔT and a steeper operating line), cold solvent, intercoolers between packed sections, or cooling coils on trays.
Closing check. Doubling the water to 516 kmol/h halves ΔT to 3.5 K, so m at the bottom is 2.28 instead of 2.56.

bank.q: A gas has Y<sub>in</sub> = 0.05 and Y<sub>out</sub> = 0.005. Equilibrium is Y* = 25X. Fresh solvent has X<sub>0</sub> = 0. Calculate the minimum L/G.
outline: X* at inlet gas = Y<sub>in</sub>/m = 0.002
operating line at minimum passes through (X*, Y<sub>in</sub>)
L/G<sub>min</sub> = (Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>)/(X* − X<sub>0</sub>)
answer 22.5
answer: Data: Y<sub>in</sub> = 0.05 and Y<sub>out</sub> = 0.005 kmol solute/kmol inert gas, X<sub>0</sub> = 0, equilibrium Y* = 25X, all mole ratios.

Sketch. Plot Y* = 25X from X = 0 to 0.002 (Y* from 0 to 0.05). Mark the top point (X<sub>0</sub>, Y<sub>out</sub>) = (0, 0.005) and the horizontal line Y = Y<sub>in</sub> = 0.05. The horizontal meets the equilibrium line at (0.002, 0.05). The straight line joining (0, 0.005) to (0.002, 0.05) is the minimum operating line; its slope is the answer. Any line from the top point with a smaller slope would cross Y* = 25X before reaching Y = 0.05.

Why mole ratios. The flows G and L used in the slope are the inert gas and the solute-free solvent, which are constant through the column, so the operating line is exactly straight on Y–X axes. Using mole fractions with total flows would bend the line slightly and shift the answer.

Where the pinch is. The equilibrium line is straight through the origin and the solvent is fresh, so at the minimum liquid rate the operating line touches the equilibrium line at the rich (bottom) end, where the leaving liquid is in equilibrium with the entering gas.
Liquid in equilibrium with the entering gas: X*<sub>1</sub> = Y<sub>in</sub>/m = 0.05/25 = 0.002 kmol solute/kmol solvent.
Minimum ratio: (L/G)<sub>min</sub> = (Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>)/(X*<sub>1</sub> − X<sub>0</sub>) = (0.05 − 0.005)/(0.002 − 0) = 0.045/0.002 = 22.5 kmol solvent/kmol inert gas.
Same result from the straight-line form: (L/G)<sub>min</sub> = m(1 − Y<sub>out</sub>/Y<sub>in</sub>) = 25 × (1 − 0.1) = 22.5.

answer.text: Check that the minimum line stays above equilibrium:

answer: Meaning. The absorption factor at the minimum is A = 22.5/25 = 0.90, equal to the fraction removed, R = 0.9: the Kremser equation gives infinite stages exactly when A = R. A real design uses 1.2 to 1.5 times the minimum.

Solvent rate. For 100 kmol/h of inert gas the minimum is 22.5 × 100 = 2250 kmol/h of solvent; at 1.5 times it is 3375 kmol/h. The large m (25) is what makes the solvent demand so high: a poorly soluble gas needs a lot of liquid.
Closing check: (L/G)<sub>min</sub> × X*<sub>1</sub> = 22.5 × 0.002 = 0.045 = Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>, so the solute balance closes.

bank.q: For the same gas, use L/G = 1.5 times the minimum and find the outlet liquid mole ratio X<sub>1</sub>.
outline: solute balance: L(X<sub>1</sub> − X<sub>0</sub>) = G(Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>)
X<sub>1</sub> = (Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>)/(L/G)
answer: Design ratio: L/G = 1.5 × 22.5 = 33.75 kmol solvent/kmol inert gas.
Solute balance over the column: L(X<sub>1</sub> − X<sub>0</sub>) = G(Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>), so X<sub>1</sub> = X<sub>0</sub> + (Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>)/(L/G).

Why the outlet liquid is weaker than the pinch value. A larger solvent flow carries the same absorbed solute (0.045 kmol per kmol inert gas) in more liquid, so X<sub>1</sub> falls in proportion: 0.045/22.5 = 0.002 at the minimum, 0.045/33.75 = 0.00133 at 1.5 times. A weaker outlet liquid also means more liquid to pump and regenerate per kmol of solute recovered.

Sketch. On the Y–X plot the design line starts at the same top point (0, 0.005) as the minimum line but is steeper, so it reaches Y = 0.05 at X = 0.00133, left of the pinch point (0.002, 0.05). The vertical gap to Y* = 25X is 0.005 at the top and 0.0167 at the bottom, never zero.
Basis. For G = 100 kmol/h of inert gas the solvent is 3375 kmol/h, and the solute absorbed is 100 × 0.045 = 4.5 kmol/h.
Outlet liquid: X<sub>1</sub> = 0 + 0.045/33.75 = 0.001333 kmol solute/kmol solvent. This is two-thirds of the pinch value 0.002, as it must be at 1.5 times the minimum.
Operating line: Y = 0.005 + 33.75X, from (0, 0.005) at the top to (0.001333, 0.05) at the bottom.

answer.text: Driving forces at the two ends:

answer: Why 1.5 times. At the minimum both N and N<sub>OG</sub> are infinite; at 1.5 times they are about 4 and 4.6. A further increase buys little: at 2 times the minimum (A = 1.8) N falls only to 2.7.
Closing check: 33.75 × 0.001333 = 0.0450 = Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>.

bank.q: A tray absorber has A = 1.4 and N = 6 theoretical stages. Use the Kremser equation to estimate the fraction of solute removed when Y<sub>in</sub> = 0.04, X<sub>0</sub> = 0 and m = 2.
outline: Kremser absorption equation for A ≠ 1
compute Y<sub>out</sub> from N, A and mX<sub>0</sub>
fraction removed = (Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>)/Y<sub>in</sub>
state assumptions: straight equilibrium and operating lines
answer: Kremser absorption equation for straight lines (A ≠ 1): (Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>)/(Y<sub>in</sub> − mX<sub>0</sub>) = (A<sup>N+1</sup> − A)/(A<sup>N+1</sup> − 1). Here Y<sub>in</sub> is the gas entering the bottom (Y<sub>N</sub>+1), Y<sub>out</sub> the gas leaving the top (Y<sub>1</sub>) and X<sub>0</sub> the solvent entering the top.
Data: A = 1.4, N = 6, Y<sub>in</sub> = 0.04, X<sub>0</sub> = 0, m = 2. Because X<sub>0</sub> = 0, mX<sub>0</sub> = 0 and the left side is simply the fraction removed.

Why the equation has this form. Writing the solute balance and equilibrium stage by stage gives Y<sub>n</sub>+1 − AY<sub>n</sub> relations that telescope into a geometric series in A; summing it gives A<sup>N+1</sup> terms. It is exact only while A is constant, that is, while L/G and m are constant.

Sketch. On Y–X axes draw Y* = 2X and the operating line from (0, 0.00168) to (0.01369, 0.04), slope 2.8. Six steps from the top fit between them, the steps growing larger towards the bottom because A > 1 opens the gap there.
Fraction removed = 95.8 %, and the gas leaves with Y<sub>out</sub> = 0.00168 kmol solute/kmol inert gas.
Liquid. L/G = Am = 1.4 × 2 = 2.8; X<sub>N</sub> = (0.04 − 0.00168)/2.8 = 0.01369 kmol solute/kmol solvent. Bottom driving force 0.04 − 2 × 0.01369 = 0.0126, top driving force 0.00168: both positive.

answer.text: How the removal grows with N at A = 1.4:

answer: Stage check by stepping (top down). Y<sub>1</sub> = 0.00168; X<sub>1</sub> = 0.00084; Y<sub>2</sub> = 0.00168 + 2.8 × 0.00084 = 0.00403; continuing gives Y<sub>3</sub> = 0.00731, Y<sub>4</sub> = 0.01191, Y<sub>5</sub> = 0.01835, Y<sub>6</sub> = 0.02737 and Y<sub>7</sub> = 0.0400 after six stages, exactly the entering gas.
Assumptions: straight equilibrium line Y* = 2X (dilute, isothermal), constant L and G on a solute-free basis, theoretical stages. For real trays divide 6 by the overall efficiency.
Closing check: with A > 1 the removal approaches 100 % as N grows; with A < 1 it could never pass A.

bank.q: A packed absorber has H<sub>OG</sub> = 0.8 m and N<sub>OG</sub> = 5.5. Find Z. State why H<sub>OG</sub> and N<sub>OG</sub> are separated in design.
outline: Z = H<sub>OG</sub> N<sub>OG</sub>
H<sub>OG</sub> contains mass-transfer coefficient and flow rates
N<sub>OG</sub> contains equilibrium and operating lines
answer: Packed height: Z = H<sub>OG</sub> × N<sub>OG</sub> = 0.8 × 5.5 = 4.4 m of packing.

Where the numbers come from. N<sub>OG</sub> = 5.5 would come from the duty, for example the straight-line formula N<sub>OG</sub> = ln[(1 − 1/A)(Y<sub>in</sub> − mX<sub>in</sub>)/(Y<sub>out</sub> − mX<sub>in</sub>) + 1/A]/(1 − 1/A). H<sub>OG</sub> = 0.8 m would come from G<sub>M</sub>/(K<sub>Ya</sub>), for example G<sub>M</sub> = 0.02 kmol/(m²·s) and K<sub>Ya</sub> = 0.025 kmol/(m³·s·ΔY), or from H<sub>G</sub> + λH<sub>L</sub> with film values.

The same split exists on the liquid side: Z = H<sub>OL</sub> × N<sub>OL</sub> with H<sub>OL</sub> = L<sub>M</sub>/(K<sub>Xa</sub>) and N<sub>OL</sub> = ∫dX/(X* − X). Use whichever pair matches the coefficient you have; for straight lines H<sub>OL</sub> = A·H<sub>OG</sub> and N<sub>OL</sub> = N<sub>OG</sub>/A give the same Z.

What H<sub>OG</sub> holds. H<sub>OG</sub> = G<sub>M</sub>/(K<sub>Ya</sub>): the inert-gas flux and the overall volumetric coefficient. It depends on the packing (through a), the flows (through the film coefficients) and the physical properties, and it changes only a little with the purity asked for. It is found from correlations or vendor data, typically 0.3 to 1 m. Its parts are H<sub>OG</sub> = H<sub>G</sub> + λH<sub>L</sub> with λ = mG/L.

What N<sub>OG</sub> holds. N<sub>OG</sub> = ∫dY/(Y − Y*) from Y<sub>out</sub> to Y<sub>in</sub>: the change in gas composition divided by the average driving force. It depends only on the equilibrium line, the operating line (L/G) and the end compositions, not on the packing.

Why separate them. (a) Each can be found on its own: N<sub>OG</sub> from the process duty and thermodynamics, H<sub>OG</sub> from the equipment. (b) A packing change alters only H<sub>OG</sub>, a purity change alters only N<sub>OG</sub>, so alternatives can be compared quickly. (c) H<sub>OG</sub> varies far less than K<sub>Ya</sub> itself, because G<sub>M</sub> and K<sub>Ya</sub> rise together with flow, so one H<sub>OG</sub> value is reliable over a range.
Built height. Add room for the distributor, support, redistributor and sump, about 1.2 m in this unit's rule: 4.4 + 1.2 = 5.6 m, built as 6.0 m (rounded up to the next half metre).
Closing check: 4.4/0.8 = 5.5 transfer units, so the arithmetic is consistent.

bank.q: A tower must handle a foaming, corrosive gas with a high liquid rate. Choose between random packing, structured packing and trays, and justify using a, ε and F<sub>p</sub>.
outline: random packing: cheap, good for corrosive service, lower capacity
structured packing: high area, low pressure drop, poor for fouling
trays: good for high liquid, fouling and heat removal
use a, ε and Fp to compare area, capacity and pressure drop
answer: The duty: foaming liquid, corrosive gas and a high liquid rate. Each one points to a different property, so judge the options with a, ε and F<sub>p</sub>.

What each number tells us here. a: transfer area per m³, so it fixes the height for a given N<sub>OG</sub>. ε: the room left for gas once the liquid hold-up is in place, so with a high liquid rate a high ε is essential. F<sub>p</sub>: read into the flooding chart with the flow parameter (L/G)(ρ_G/ρ_L)<sup>0</sup>.5; a high liquid rate gives a large flow parameter and a low flooding gas rate, made worse by a high F<sub>p</sub>.

Foaming. Trays make foam by bubbling gas through a liquid pool; the froth fills the tray spacing and floods early. Packing spreads liquid as thin films with gentle contact, so packing handles foaming far better. Trays are ruled out unless antifoam can be used.

Corrosion. Random packings come in ceramic and plastic (PP, PVDF), both cheap and corrosion resistant. Structured packings are mostly thin metal sheet or gauze, and corrosion-resistant alloys or plastic structured packings cost much more. Thin metal also fails first in corrosive service.

High liquid rate. A high liquid rate fills the voids and lowers the flooding gas rate. A packing with high ε and a low F<sub>p</sub> keeps capacity; structured packing has the highest ε but its narrow channels can hold up foam at high liquid loads; large random rings (Pall rings or saddles, 50 mm) have high ε and modest F<sub>p</sub>.

head: Option
a, m²/m³
ε
F<sub>p</sub>
Verdict
rows: resists corrosion, high capacity, tolerates foam
best area; costly in alloy, poor with foam

answer: Recommendation: random packing of 50 mm plastic Pall rings or saddles (ceramic if the temperature is too high for plastic). It resists the corrosive gas, its high void fraction and low packing factor take the high liquid rate without early flooding, and it does not foam the liquid.

Price paid: lower a than 25 mm rings or structured packing, so the bed is taller. With a ≈ 100 against 200 m²/m³ the bed may need about twice the height for the same N<sub>OG</sub> if H<sub>OG</sub> scales with 1/a, which is usually cheaper than the alloy.
Closing check: design at 50 to 70 % of flooding and add a good distributor and redistributors every few metres to keep the high liquid flow spread evenly.

bank.q: Compare tray and packed absorbers for recovery, pressure drop, turndown and maintenance. Recommend one for a service with corrosive solvent and frequent cleaning.
outline: tray: discrete stages, easy cleaning, higher pressure drop
packed: low pressure drop, high area, but cleaning difficult
corrosive service favours plastic or ceramic packing or trays
frequent cleaning favours trays or large-pitch packing
recommendation with reasons
answer: Recovery (separation). Both can reach any recovery if they are tall enough: trays by adding stages (N/E<sub>o</sub> real trays), packing by adding height (H<sub>OG</sub> × N<sub>OG</sub>, or HETP × N). Neither is better in principle; efficiency data decide the height.

Liquid hold-up. Trays hold more liquid than packing. That helps when a slow liquid-phase reaction needs residence time, but it is a disadvantage for heat-sensitive or hazardous liquids, where a small inventory is safer. Trays also allow cooling coils and side draws on chosen trays, which helps non-isothermal absorption.
Diameter. For large columns (over about 1 m) trays are usually cheaper per unit of capacity; for small ones packing is cheaper and easier to install.

Pressure drop. Gas must lift the liquid pool on each tray, typically several hundred pascals per tray. Packed beds run at about 15 to 50 mm of water per metre of packing (about 150 to 500 Pa/m). Packing wins wherever fan or compressor power matters or the gas is at low pressure.
Turndown. Valve and bubble-cap trays work over a wide range of rates. Packed beds lose wetting and suffer maldistribution at low liquid rates. Trays win where flows vary widely.

Maintenance and cleaning. Trays have manways; a worker can enter, clean and inspect each tray, and trays tolerate solids. Packing must be removed and replaced to be cleaned, and solids plug it. Trays win where fouling or frequent cleaning is expected.
Corrosive solvent and frequent cleaning pull in opposite directions: corrosion favours ceramic or plastic packing, cleaning favours trays.

Recommendation: a tray tower with sieve or valve trays in a corrosion-resistant alloy (or a lined shell with plastic-compatible internals where the temperature allows). Frequent cleaning is a cost that recurs every shutdown, while the alloy is paid for once; trays can be cleaned in place through manways without removing anything, and they handle any solids that make the cleaning necessary.
When to change the answer: if the diameter is below about 0.6 m, or the gas pressure drop is limited, use random plastic packing in removable sections instead.

Closing check with numbers: a 20-tray column at about 0.7 kPa per tray loses about 14 kPa; 8 m of packing at 0.3 kPa/m loses about 2.4 kPa. Accept the higher pressure drop only if the fan can supply it.

bank.q: Analyse the effect of exothermic absorption on column design. Explain when an isothermal design is unsafe and how a non-isothermal design changes the operating and equilibrium lines.
outline: heat of solution raises liquid temperature
m rises with temperature so the equilibrium line steepens
operating line changes if liquid rate or temperature changes
driving force falls, so more height or area is needed
isothermal design is unsafe for high heat of solution and concentrated solute
answer: Heat release. Each kmol absorbed releases ΔH<sub>s</sub> (heat of solution plus latent heat for a vapour). The liquid warms by ΔT = (absorbed × ΔH<sub>s</sub>)/(liquid flow × c<sub>p</sub>) if little heat is lost.

Effect on the two lines in a sketch: draw Y* = 2X dashed (cold) and a curve leaving it at the origin and rising to m = 2.56 at X = 0.0175. The operating line from (0, 0.00503) to (0.0175, 0.0526) is unchanged. The gap between the operating line and the curve shrinks steadily towards the bottom, which is the picture examiners look for.

Equilibrium line. H and m = H/P rise with temperature, so the equilibrium line steepens where the liquid is warm. The liquid is coolest at the top and warmest at the bottom, so the line curves upward towards the rich end.
Operating line. On Y–X axes with solute-free flows the operating line stays straight; it moves only if the designer changes L/G (for example, more solvent to cool the liquid).

answer.pre:
ΔT = 4.52 × 30 000 / (258 × 18 × 4.18) = 7.0 K
m: 2.00 at the top → 2.56 at the bottom
bottom gap: 0.0176 (isothermal) → 0.0078 (adiabatic)
N<sub>OG</sub>:       4.75 → 6.06   (Simpson over seven points)
bed:        1.42 → 1.82 m with H<sub>OG</sub> = 0.30 m

answer: Driving force. Less than half the isothermal gap remains at the bottom, so N<sub>OG</sub> grows by 28 %. An isothermal design of 1.42 m would deliver less than the specified recovery.

When an isothermal design is unsafe: (a) a large heat of solution (HCl, NH₃, SO₂, amine–CO₂, condensing vapours); (b) a rich gas, so much solute is absorbed per kmol of liquid; (c) a solvent rate close to the minimum, where the small gap can close completely; (d) a small liquid-to-gas ratio, so the liquid has little heat capacity. A quick test: if ΔT changes m by more than about 10 %, design non-isothermally.

How the design changes. Step stages or integrate the height with a heat balance carried alongside the mass balance, reading m at each local temperature. Remedies: more or colder solvent, intercoolers between packed sections, cooling coils on trays.
Closing check. With twice the water (L/G = 5.43) ΔT = 3.5 K and m(bottom) = 2.28; the operating line is steeper too, so the bottom gap opens to 0.0526 − 2.28 × 0.00876 = 0.0326.

bank.q: Evaluate multicomponent absorption with a reacting solvent. Explain why one equilibrium line is not enough, how solutes compete, and what the enhancement factor changes.
outline: each solute has its own m and equilibrium line
write a solute balance for each component with a common solvent
competition for solvent lowers driving force for some components
reaction consumes solute and raises rate
E = rate with reaction ÷ physical rate
E depends on kinetics, concentration and contact time
answer: One equilibrium line per solute. Each solute i has its own Henry constant and slope m<sub>i</sub>, so on Y–X axes each has its own line Y<sub>i</sub>* = m<sub>iX</sub>_i. An average m would over-absorb some solutes and under-absorb others.

One operating ratio for all. All solutes share one gas stream and one liquid stream, so L/G is the same for every component; each component has its own absorption factor A<sub>i</sub> = L/(m<sub>iG</sub>).

Component balances. For each solute, G(Y<sub>i,in</sub> − Y<sub>i,out</sub>) = L(X<sub>i,out</sub> − X<sub>i,in</sub>). With straight lines, the fraction of i absorbed in N stages is (A<sub>i</sub><sup>N+1</sup> − A<sub>i</sub>)/(A<sub>i</sub><sup>N+1</sup> − 1).

How solutes compete. Solutes with A<sub>i</sub> well above 1 are almost fully absorbed; those with A<sub>i</sub> below 1 are capped near A<sub>i</sub>. The specified (key) solute fixes L/G and N, and the others take what those give. In a concentrated system the absorbed solutes also warm the liquid and swell its flow, which shifts every m<sub>i</sub>; and a solute that reacts uses up the solvent's reagent, leaving less for the others.

Reaction. A reacting solvent consumes the dissolved solute, keeping its concentration low, so the back pressure is near zero (y* ≈ 0) and the solvent capacity rises. The enhancement factor E = (flux with reaction)/(physical flux at the same interfacial concentration) measures the gain in rate.

What E depends on. Ha = √(kD<sub>A</sub>)/k<sub>L</sub>. Slow (Ha < 0.3): E ≈ 1. Fast (3 < Ha ≪ E<sub>i</sub>): E ≈ Ha, for example Ha = 20 gives a flux 20 × 6 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ kmol/(m²·s). Instantaneous: E = E<sub>i</sub> = 1 + D<sub>Bc</sub>_B/(bD<sub>Ac</sub>_Ai), for example 6. E therefore depends on kinetics (k), reagent concentration (c<sub>B</sub>) and contact time (through k<sub>L</sub>).

Selectivity. Each solute has its own Ha<sub>i</sub> and E<sub>i</sub>, so a solvent can take H₂S (instantaneous with amines) much faster than CO₂ (finite rate): selectivity comes from kinetics, which short contact times exploit.

Evaluation. Multicomponent design needs one equilibrium line per solute, one L/G and a key component; reaction adds one enhancement factor per solute. Closing check: 2.21 + 3.51 + 2.93 + 1.00 = 9.65 kmol/h absorbed of 17 kmol/h of solutes.

bank.q: Evaluate the idea of operating an absorber at the minimum liquid-to-gas ratio. Include pinch, column height and solvent pumping cost.
outline: at minimum L/G the operating line touches equilibrium at the pinch
driving force is zero at the pinch so height becomes infinite
operate above minimum, commonly 1.2 to 2 times
more liquid lowers stage height but raises pumping and regeneration cost
optimum balances capital and operating cost
answer: Minimum L/G. Lowering the solvent rate turns the operating line down about the fixed top point until it touches the equilibrium line: the pinch. For the acetone example (Y<sub>in</sub> = 0.0526, Y<sub>out</sub> = 0.00503, Y* = 2X) (L/G)<sub>min</sub> = 0.04757/0.0263 = 1.809.

Height at the pinch. The driving force Y − Y* is zero at the pinch, so ∫dY/(Y − Y*) diverges: infinite stages, infinite height. Below the minimum the lines cross and the specification cannot be met at any height.

Where the pinch is. For a straight equilibrium line through the origin with fresh solvent, the gap Y<sub>out</sub> + (L/G − m)X falls as X rises whenever L/G < m, so the pinch is at the bottom (rich end). With a curved equilibrium line the pinch can be a tangent part way up the column, and the minimum must be found by checking every X.

Diameter and flooding. More solvent also raises the liquid load on the packing, lowers the flooding gas rate and so widens the column; at 3 times the minimum the liquid flow is 515.5 kmol/h against 257.7 at 1.5 times, which can force a larger diameter even though the bed is shorter.

answer.text: How N<sub>OG</sub> and bed height (H<sub>OG</sub> = 0.30 m) depend on L/G:

answer: Capital cost. Near the minimum the height rises steeply: going from 1.2 to 1.05 times the minimum saves 12 % of the solvent but nearly doubles the bed.

Operating cost. Solvent must be pumped, then regenerated in a stripper, which needs heat roughly in proportion to the solvent flow. Above about 2 times the minimum the bed shrinks little (1.11 → 0.92 m from 2 to 3 times) while the solvent rate rises by half.

Risk. At 1.05 times the minimum a small rise in temperature (m up a few per cent) or in gas rate closes the gap and the outlet goes off specification. The heat-effects example showed m rising 28 % at the bottom, which alone would cross a near-minimum line.
Optimum. Total annual cost = capital (height, diameter) + solvent pumping and regeneration. The usual optimum lies at 1.2 to 1.5 times the minimum (absorption factor 1.25 to 1.5).
Verdict: operating at the minimum is not possible (infinite height) and operating close to it is unwise; choose about 1.5 times, here L = 257.7 kmol/h with a 1.43 m bed.
Closing check: at 1.5 times, X<sub>out</sub> = 0.04757/2.713 = 0.0175, two-thirds of the pinch value 0.0263.

glossary.def: Transfer of one or more gas components into a liquid solvent.
Removal of dissolved gas from a liquid by contact with a gas lean in that solute.
Moles of solute per mole of carrier gas or solvent, excluding the solute itself.
At equilibrium the partial pressure of a gas equals a constant times its liquid mole fraction.
The locus of gas compositions in equilibrium with liquid compositions at a fixed temperature and pressure.
The locus of gas and liquid compositions that satisfy the solute balance in a contactor.
The difference between actual composition and equilibrium composition at a point in the contactor.
A point where the operating line meets the equilibrium line, making the driving force zero.
The smallest solvent flow per gas flow that can achieve a specified separation.
An ideal contact stage in which outgoing gas and liquid are in equilibrium.
Ratio of actual solute removed on a tray to solute removed by an ideal theoretical stage.
A = L/(mG), the operating-line slope L/G divided by the equilibrium slope m.
A formula relating the number of stages, absorption factor and solute recovery for straight lines.
Total surface of the packing per unit volume of packed bed, usually m²/m³.
The fraction of the packed-bed volume that is empty space.
An empirical number for a packing used to estimate pressure drop and capacity.
Height equivalent to a theoretical plate, the packed height per equilibrium stage.

glossary.term: Height of an overall gas-phase transfer unit
glossary.def: H<sub>OG</sub>, the packed height that gives one overall gas-phase transfer unit.

glossary.term: Number of overall gas-phase transfer units
glossary.def: N<sub>OG</sub>, the dimensionless separation duty obtained from equilibrium and operating lines.
K<sub>Ya</sub>, the overall gas-phase coefficient multiplied by the interfacial area per unit bed volume.
Absorption in which heat release changes the liquid temperature and therefore the solubility.
E = actual absorption rate with reaction ÷ physical absorption rate without reaction.
Absorption in which the dissolved solute reacts chemically with the solvent or a reagent in it.
Absorption of two or more solutes into one solvent, where each solute has its own equilibrium line.
Ha = √(kD<sub>A</sub>)/k<sub>L</sub>, the ratio of reaction in the liquid film to diffusion through it.
S = mG/L = 1/A, the stripping counterpart of the absorption factor.
